title: Home to his mother
hook: the baby refuses every nurse until his sister leads them to his own mother

segments.voice: Yesterday: Asiya's arms, and a queen who said do not kill him. Your line was a good heart in a hard house. Did you bring one kindness somewhere hard? Day forty-five.
screen: `A GOOD HEART IN A HARD HOUSE.`

segments.voice: Back upstream, in a small house, a mother is sitting very still. She's done it. She's set her son on the river. And now the Qur'an gives us one of its most honest lines about what that costs. It says the heart of Musa's mother became empty. Hollowed out. So empty she nearly gave the whole secret away, and would have, the verse says, if Allah hadn't strengthened her heart. Anyone who has waited by a phone for news knows that emptiness. But she doesn't just sit. She turns to her daughter, Musa's sister, and gives her one word. Follow him. Today: home to his mother.
screen: `A HEART GONE EMPTY.` → `SHE NEARLY TELLS.` → `FOLLOW HIM.`

segments.voice: Surah al-Qasas keeps going. The sister watches from a distance, the Qur'an says, while they didn't notice her. Picture a girl on the edge of a crowd at the palace, trying to look like she's just passing by. Meanwhile, inside, there's a problem. The baby won't nurse. Nurse after nurse is brought in, and he turns away from every one. The Qur'an says Allah had forbidden him the foster mothers beforehand. Something in him refuses. And the sister sees her chance. She steps forward and says, as innocently as she can: shall I show you a household who will raise him for you and take good care of him? And so, the verse says, We returned him to his mother, so that her eye might be cooled, and she would not grieve, and so she would know that the promise of Allah is true. Remember day forty-three? When she put him on the river, she was promised: We will bring him back to you. Here it is, a few verses later. There's yesterday's image again too: her eye cooled. The same delight Asiya felt, now given back to the woman who bore him. And notice who makes it happen. Not an army. Not a miracle anyone can see. A baby who won't feed, and a sister brave enough to speak up at the right moment. The Qur'an doesn't give the sister's name, and the sources are quiet about her after this. But without her, no homecoming. Some commentators add that the mother was even paid to nurse her own son. The text itself only says he came home.
screen: `THE SISTER WATCHES FROM AFAR.` · `HE REFUSES EVERY NURSE.` · `SHALL I SHOW YOU A HOUSEHOLD?` · `THE PROMISE KEPT.` · then, large: `HER EYE COOLED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice how something came back to you. Settle, and breathe. Think back over your life for something you lost, or let go of, or gave up on, that found its way back. A friendship that restarted after years. A thing you misplaced for a month. A sense of humor after a bad season. Your appetite for something you used to love. Let it come back into your mind, and notice who or what carried it home. Often it's someone small, standing on the edge of the crowd. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. The bell holds the time.
Home to his mother. A baby who refused every nurse, a sister who spoke up, and a promise kept. Today's word.
Your line: what is yours returns. Today, thank one person who once carried something back to you, even if it was years ago. Day forty-five.

howItsDone: Muslims often point to Musa's return to his mother as a sign that Allah's promises are kept, and the story is a favorite in teaching children about trust and family.

match.prompt: who did what in the story — tap the pairs.
pairs: We will bring him back to you

myth: she is unnamed, and the sources say little about her after this.
the Qur'an admits his mother nearly gave the secret away
her heart became empty, and she nearly revealed it, until Allah strengthened her heart.
the palace found his mother by searching the city
his sister stepped forward and offered a household who would raise him.

fork.setup: you're Musa's sister, watching from the edge of the crowd. the baby won't nurse from anyone they bring. what do you do?
options: run home and tell your mother to hide.
step forward and offer a household who will care for him.
keep watching. it isn't safe to speak.
fork.reveal: she said: shall I show you a household who will raise him and take good care of him? and so he came home to his mother, just as she'd been promised.

original.note: Arabic, from Qur'an 28:10: "empty" — the heart of Musa's mother after she let him go.

trapdoor: what you thought: a lucky coincidence.
what it means: a promise kept. the baby refuses every nurse, his sister speaks up, and he is brought home, as his mother was told he would be.
what a scholar hears: 28:13 says he was returned "so that her eye might be cooled," the same image, from the same root, as Asiya's qurratu 'ayn a few verses earlier.

sources.ref: Qur'an 20:40 (the sister: shall I show you one who will nurse him?)

notes: The sister is unnamed in the Qur'an; commentators give names (e.g. Maryam or Kulthum). The script says only that she is unnamed and the sources say little more.
'Some commentators add that the mother was paid to nurse her own son': reported in tafsir; flagged as commentary. Confirm or remove.

Trapdoor link between 28:9 (qurratu 'ayn for Asiya) and 28:13 (taqarra 'aynuha for the mother): same root and image, not the identical phrase; the floor says 'the same image, from the same root'. Confirm.
